Prepare Event Log Data for Network Estimation

Source: R/prepare_data.R
prepare.Rd

prepare() turns an event log (one row per event: the action, and optionally who did it and when) into sequences, one row per session and one column per position (T1, T2, ...). It parses the timestamps, orders the events, splits each actor's events into sessions by explicit session columns and by time gaps, and keeps every other column as one row of metadata per session. build_network() runs the same preparation itself when given action, with the same arguments, so prepare() is for inspecting the sequences or passing them to the sequence verbs.

Usage

prepare(
  data,
  actor,
  action,
  time = NULL,
  order = NULL,
  session = NULL,
  time_threshold = 900,
  custom_format = NULL,
  is_unix_time = FALSE,
  unix_time_unit = c("seconds", "milliseconds", "microseconds"),
  timezone = "UTC"
)

# S3 method for class 'nestimate_data'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

data

The event log: a data frame with one row per event.

actor

The column, or columns, identifying who performed each event (e.g. "student" or c("student", "group")); several columns are combined, each observed combination being one actor. Missing or NULL treats all events as one actor.

action

The column holding each event's action (state or code).

time

The timestamp column. Default NULL, in which case the row order (or order) gives the order of the events and no session is split by time. Numeric values are read as Unix timestamps, and POSIXct and POSIXlt values are used as they are, in their own time zone. Text may be ISO 8601 (with Z or an offset), YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM[:SS] with -, / or ., day-first or month-first dates, dates with month names, or compact YYYYMMDDHHMMSS, more than 40 layouts in all; text that matches none but reads as a number is taken as a Unix timestamp. A value must match a layout completely, with a four-digit year, so a two-digit year raises an error of class nestimate_bad_input instead of being misread, as does any value no layout reads. Day-first or month-first is decided once for the whole column: any first field above 12 means day-first, any second field above 12 means month-first. When the column cannot decide, values are read day-first with a warning of class nestimate_ambiguous_dates; custom_format settles it. An empty or missing timestamp is not an error: that event is sorted after its session's timed events and starts a session of its own.

order

The column that orders the events: with time, it breaks ties between events with the same timestamp; without time, it gives the order of each session's events. Default NULL (the row order).

session

The column, or columns, identifying explicit sessions (e.g. "course" or c("course", "semester")). Each actor's events in one session form a sequence, further split by time gaps when time is set. Default NULL.

time_threshold

The longest gap, in seconds, between consecutive events of one session; a longer gap starts a new session, numbered s1, s2, ... within its actor and session. Used only with time. FALSE turns the split off, so each actor (or actor-session) forms one sequence however long the gaps. Default 900 (15 minutes).

custom_format

A strptime() format tried before the built-in layouts; values it does not match fall through to them. Default NULL.

is_unix_time

Whether time holds Unix timestamps. TRUE reads a text column as numbers and never as a date layout (a 12- or 14-digit value would otherwise match the compact YYYYMMDDHHMM[SS] layouts); a value that is not a number then raises an error of class nestimate_bad_input. With FALSE (default), text is matched to the date layouts first and read as a Unix timestamp only when it matches none. A numeric time column is always read as Unix timestamps.

unix_time_unit

The unit of Unix timestamps: "seconds" (default), "milliseconds" or "microseconds". A numeric time column that gives dates after the year 2500 raises a warning of class nestimate_time_unit, the usual sign of the wrong unit.

timezone

The Olson time zone (see OlsonNames()) in which timestamps without zone information are read and Unix timestamps are expressed. Timestamps that end in Z, UTC, GMT or a numeric offset such as +02:00 are converted from that offset, so parsing does not depend on the machine's time zone. Default "UTC".

x

For the print() method: a nestimate_data object.

...

Not used.

Value

A nestimate_data object. print() gives the numbers of sessions and actions, the longest sequence, the number of actors when actor was given and whether times were parsed, and returns its input invisibly. extract_sequences(), sequence_patterns() and sequence_metrics() read it directly. It holds:

sequence_data

The sequences as a data frame: one row per session, one column per position (T1, T2, ...), padded with NA.

long_data

The events in their sorted order, with the parsed time and the working columns that identify each event's session and position (.session_id, .session_label, .sequence, ...).

meta_data

One row per session, in the row order of sequence_data: .session_id, .session_label, the actor column (with several, their combined label .actor, joined by "-", or by the first of "|", " | ", " / ", " :: " that keeps distinct actors apart when values contain "-"), the session column(s) under their own names, and every other column aggregated per session.

time_data

The parsed times in the layout of sequence_data (columns time_T1, time_T2, ...), in timezone (or the zone of a date-time time column), or NULL without time.

statistics

A list with total_sessions, total_actions and max_sequence_length, plus unique_actors (distinct combinations of the actor columns) only when actor was given (without it, every event belongs to one actor).

Details

Within each actor and session, events are sorted by time and then by order. Sessions are identified by the observed combinations of the actor and session values, so identifiers containing separator characters stay distinct and high-cardinality identifiers cannot overflow. A missing value in any of these columns raises an error of class nestimate_bad_input: drop or relabel those events first.

Every other column is aggregated into the session metadata: numeric columns by their mean, other columns by their most frequent value. A tie goes to the tied value that occurs first in the session, and a message names the columns where that happened.

See also

build_network

Examples

set.seed(1)
df <- data.frame(
  student = rep(1:3, each = 5),
  code = sample(c("read", "write", "test"), 15, replace = TRUE),
  timestamp = seq.POSIXt(as.POSIXct("2024-01-01"), by = "min", length.out = 15)
)
prepared <- prepare(df, actor = "student", action = "code",
                    time = "timestamp")
prepared
#> Prepared Data for Network Estimation
#>   Sessions: 3  |  Actions: 15  |  Max length: 5
#>   Actors: 3
#>   Time data: available

# build_network() runs the same preparation itself
net <- build_network(df, actor = "student", action = "code",
                     time = "timestamp", method = "relative")
net
#> Transition Network (relative probabilities) [directed]
#>   Weights: [0.200, 0.500]  |  mean: 0.333
#> 
#>   Weight matrix:
#>          read  test write
#>   read  0.400 0.200 0.400
#>   test  0.500 0.250 0.250
#>   write 0.333 0.333 0.333 
#> 
#>   Initial probabilities:
#>   test          0.667  ████████████████████████████████████████
#>   read          0.333  ████████████████████
#>   write         0.000
